title: KV cache management investigation — reuse, eviction, paging, memory bandwidth (June 2026)
content:
Summary:

We ran a focused set of experiments to understand KV cache behavior under mixed production-like workloads and to isolate the dominant bottlenecks that lead to higher tail latency: reuse (hit) rates, eviction dynamics, OS-level paging, and memory bandwidth saturation. The goal was to compare three cache strategies (baseline LRU, LFU-like aging, and pinned+prefetch) across realistic request mixes and quantify tradeoffs (latency, throughput, resource utilization).

Background & motivation:

Recent customer reports and SLO traces show intermittent P99 latency spikes during heavy multi-tenant bursts. Preliminary traces implicated high KV cache churn (low reuse) and occasional OS page faults when host memory approaches capacity. We need concrete numbers to decide whether to: 1) increase cache sizes, 2) change eviction policy, 3) add pinning/prefetch, or 4) tune OS/kernel settings.

Hypothesis:

1) A frequency-aware policy (LFU with aging) will increase reuse and reduce eviction churn relative to LRU for our mixed short/long-context workload.
2) Pinning hot shards and prefetching expected KV ranges will maximize reuse but increase sustained memory bandwidth consumption — this may trade lower latency for higher resource use.
3) When host memory use >~85% we will see page-in activity cause large latency outliers; lowering swappiness/controlling allocation should reduce those spikes.

Experiment setup:

- Hardware: 8x A100 (80GB) worker nodes used for model inference; control-plane/host processes on 2x c6i.8xlarge-like instances for the cache manager. Tests run on staging cluster that mirrors production topology.
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes derived from sampled production traces: 
  * Mix A (conversational-heavy): 60% long-context (>2k tokens), 40% short (<256 tokens)
  * Mix B (short-heavy): 80% short, 20% medium (512–1024 tokens)
  * Mix C (bursting multi-tenant): many warm-up short requests across 200 tenants (hot-key pattern)
- Cache configs: all runs used a single-node logical cache size target (host memory-backed) to emulate Dedicated nodes. Variants: 
  * Baseline-LRU: 24 GB cache, LRU eviction, no prefetch
  * LFU-Aging: 24 GB cache, frequency weights with exponential aging (half-life 10m), periodic decays
  * Pinned+Prefetch: 40 GB effective (pin top 10% hottest shards), prefetcher that triggers on tenant affinity
- Measurement: per-request KV hit/miss, eviction events/s, page-in events (OS), memory bandwidth sampled via perf and node-exporter (reported GB/s), latency percentiles (P50/P90/P99), throughput (reqs/s). Each experiment ran for 90 minutes after warm-up.

Key metrics and definitions:

- reuse_rate: KV hits / total KV lookups (reported as %).
- eviction_rate: number of cache item evictions per second.
- paging_events: OS major page faults per million requests (normalized).
- memory_bandwidth: sustained read/write bandwidth attributable to KV ops measured (GB/s).
- latency_p99: 99th percentile end-to-end inference latency (ms).

Results (aggregated across mixes):

Baseline-LRU (24GB):
- reuse_rate: 42% (Mix A: 35%, Mix B: 58%, Mix C: 30%)
- eviction_rate: 18 evictions/s average (peaks 45/s during bursts)
- paging_events: low overall, but non-zero during long Mix A tails when node memory >85% (0.7 major faults / 1e6 reqs)
- memory_bandwidth: 48 GB/s (tail spikes to 80 GB/s during eviction sweeps)
- latency: P50 = 28 ms, P90 = 55 ms, P99 = 95 ms

LFU-Aging (24GB):
- reuse_rate: 58% (Mix A: 50%, Mix B: 72%, Mix C: 55%)
- eviction_rate: 9 evictions/s average (peaks 18/s)
- paging_events: reduced compared to baseline (0.2 major faults / 1e6 reqs)
- memory_bandwidth: 62 GB/s (more read-dominant due to repeated hot-key hits)
- latency: P50 = 24 ms, P90 = 40 ms, P99 = 70 ms

Pinned+Prefetch (40GB):
- reuse_rate: 75% (Mix A: 68%, Mix B: 88%, Mix C: 80%)
- eviction_rate: 2 evictions/s average (very rare)
- paging_events: near-zero (pinning avoided OS-level page reclaim in hot set)
- memory_bandwidth: 110 GB/s sustained (higher due to prefetch + pinned hot-range scans)
- latency: P50 = 20 ms, P90 = 32 ms, P99 = 45 ms

Observations & interpretation:

1) LFU-Aging provides a large win over naive LRU with no config changes. Reuse increases ~+16pp on average and P99 drops by ~25 ms. Eviction churn is reduced, leading to fewer background eviction-related memory bursts.
2) Pinned+Prefetch is best for tail latency and almost eliminates evictions, but it increases sustained memory bandwidth by ~2x relative to LFU. This is a classical tradeoff: lower tail latency at the cost of higher host IO. On nodes where memory BW is already a constraint, this can cause contention with other subsystems (e.g., model weight swaps).
3) Paging/OS-level faults are rare at moderate memory utilization but become the dominant source of extreme P99 spikes when memory crosses ~85% utilization. In those cases even a handful of major page-ins adds hundreds of ms to latency.
4) Mix-dependent behavior: short-heavy mixes benefit most from pinning and LFU since hot keys surface quickly. Conversational workloads (long context) still show lower reuse due to many unique KV sequences.

Root causes identified:

- Hot vs transient keys: many tenants generate short-lived keys causing LRU thrash; frequency-aware retention distinguishes true hot keys.
- Cache sizing mismatch: default 24GB is often insufficient for pinned hot sets during mixed bursts; autoscaling cache capacity or node placement required.
- OS settings: default swappiness and transparent hugepages behavior lead to occasional major faults under peak allocation churn.
- Memory bandwidth constraints: prefetching increases steady-state bandwidth and can starve other memory-heavy operations on the node.

Recommendations (short-term & medium-term):

Short-term (actionable, low-risk):
- Roll out LFU-Aging as the default eviction policy behind a lab feature flag (SERV-1423). This requires a small runtime config change and a telemetry spike for per-shard reuse metrics (see linked PR).
- Add mem_util and pagefault alerts: trigger at 75%/85% thresholds to warn before heavy swapping.
- Lower system swappiness on Dedicated hosts to 10 and re-run smoke tests (reduces major page-ins).
- Add eviction/compaction smoothing to avoid large eviction sweeps that cause transient memory BW spikes.

Medium-term (risky / higher-effort):
- Implement hot-key pinning with a tenant-aware prefetcher (start with conservative prefetch budget; patch PR submitted: PR #4567). Measure end-to-end system memory BW before enabling widely.
- Autosize cache per-tenant or per-shard using observed reuse telemetry; prefer vertical scaling of cache node rather than global fixed-size config for multi-tenant mixing.
- Expose per-shard KV reuse and eviction metrics in Console dashboards (per-route/tenant view) and add regression alerts in Redwood Optimize.

Experiments to run next:

- Controlled LFU parameter sweep (half-life 1m/5m/10m/30m) to find sweet spot per workload family (Mix A vs Mix B).
- Prefetch budget test (5/10/20% of cache BW) to find knee of diminishing returns for latency vs BW.
- Node placement policy: colocate long-context heavy tenants on nodes with larger cache or dedicated pinning to reduce cross-tenant thrash.

Action items & owners:

- Aisha: deploy LFU-Aging behind feature flag in staging + collect 48h telemetry (due 2026-07-09).
- Liam: add mem/pagefault alerts and dashboard tiles for per-node KV BS/mem BW (due 2026-07-05).
- Ravi: open kernel tuning PR to set swappiness=10 in init scripts and add a rollback plan (PR and testing by 2026-07-12).
- Sofia: prototype hot-key pinning prefetch with conservative budget on 2 nodes and report BW/latency impact (due 2026-07-16).

Notes / open questions:

- Need to validate pinned+prefetch impact on customers that also perform large model weight swaps on the same host (possible BW contention).
- Is a hybrid approach (LFU + small pinned set) the practical default? Likely yes, but requires careful telemetry and an adaptive algorithm.
- Should we expose a tenant-level cache_hint API so customers can mark keys as hot (for model-directed pinning)? This would be a product/console decision.

References & linked artifacts:

- Jira: SERV-1423 (KV cache eviction tuning)
- Confluence: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/123456789/kv-cache-investigation
- Runtime PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4567
- Slack thread with perf traces: slack://channel/C01234567/p1623456789000

Appendix: raw metric snapshots (selected)

- Mix A, Baseline-LRU snapshot (30 min steady-state): reuse 35%; evictions 32/s (burst windows); mem BW 68 GB/s peak; page-in spikes correlated with 3 P99 events >300ms.
- Mix B, LFU-Aging snapshot: reuse 72%; evictions 6/s; mem BW 52 GB/s steady; P99 48ms.
- Mix C, Pinned+Prefetch snapshot: reuse 80%; evictions 0–1/s; mem BW 118 GB/s sustained; P99 40ms.

If reviewers want raw logs/CSV exports and perf traces I uploaded the artifacts to the investigation folder in Confluence and attached the main flamegraphs to PR #4567.
